cultural.vision_reason: The image shows a hand-woven, strip-sewn cotton boubou/tobe gown with traditional embroidery, a garment style shared across West African Sahelian peoples including Wolof; it is plausible dress for the claimed group even if the "two knives" motif is more commonly associated with Hausa work, since neighboring traditions overlap and are not distinguishable here.

physical.title: gown; textile; tobe
physical.summary: Man’s gown (boubou, tobe, riga), hand-woven from hand-spun white cotton. The body is formed of 116 narrow strips hand-sewn together along the selvedges vertically, while the sleeves are sewn horizontally. The body of the gown is rectangular in shape, while the sleeves flare out being wider at the top than at the bottom. At the front is sewn a large pocket. The gown is hand-embroidered in the ‘two knives’ (aska biyu) pattern. The two knives and the area around the neck are embroidered with a silk-like thread (possibly a  local silk thread, tsamiya); the rest of the decoration (five squares and two spirals (tambari), one on the front and one on the back) are in the same white cotton as the body of the gown, and are in chain and buttonhole eyelet stitching. The sleeves of the garment are sewn with a hem; the neck and bottom are not.
